claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch enhances local lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortion is the dominant mechanism impeding dislocation motion when processing and microstructural features are nearly identical.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by lattice distortion increases hardness and yield strength.
The comparison should use as-cast or homogenized alloys with consistent grain size, phase distribution, and precipitate content.

Substituting an element with one having a significantly different atomic radius but similar chemical or electronic character will increase the calculated lattice-distortion parameter while otherwise preserving the comparison.
Alloy pairs should be processed identically and differ primarily in atomic size mismatch.
Greater atomic size mismatch creates larger local stress fields.
Larger local stress fields hinder dislocation motion.
Holding grain size and phase content constant isolates lattice distortion as the source of strengthening.
Alloys with a higher calculated lattice-distortion parameter will have proportionately higher hardness and yield strength than the baseline.
Minimal compositional complexity implies minimal atomic-size differences and lower lattice-distortion strengthening.
The hypothesis is limited to controlled single-phase or dual-phase alloys in which secondary phases, grain boundaries, and precipitates do not dominate the mechanical response.
Phase constitution can independently affect strengthening, so secondary-phase effects must be minimized in the proposed comparison.
The quantitative contribution of lattice distortion relative to other strengthening mechanisms is uncertain, especially at elevated temperature or very high compositional complexity.
An absent, statistically insignificant, or reversed relationship between lattice-distortion parameter and both hardness and yield strength would falsify the hypothesis.
